301	                                                    This study aimed to use video analysis to assess trends in the ACL injury mechanisms of American football
302	                                                    players. The kinematics most commonly encountered with ACL injuries were deceleration, mild knee flexion
303	                                                    (0°-30°), and initial foot-to-ground contact through heel strike. Additionally, most injuries were associated
304	                                                    with contact from another athlete, either directly to the knee or indirectly to other parts of the body.
305	
306	
307	                                                    Similar to previous soccer literature, most players we analyzed were decelerating at the time of injury [13].
308	                                                    However, this is discordant with Johnston et al., who previously noted that only 10% of ACL injuries in
309	                                                    professional American football players were associated with deceleration [12]. Unfortunately, the majority of
310	                                                    video analyses of sports-related injuries do not assess this crucial injury characteristic. Numerous studies
311	                                                    have examined the forces placed on the ACL during a single-leg landing during various actions and
312	                                                    confirmed that increased tension is placed on the ACL during deceleration [14-16]. Several hypotheses have
313	                                                    been proposed to explain this biomechanical correlation. One theory purports that deceleration places
314	                                                    substantial stress on the ACL in an effort to prevent anterior tibial translation [17]. Another asserts that
315	                                                    eccentric quadriceps contraction, as with deceleration, increases the compressive vector within the knee,
316	                                                    effectively lowering the injury threshold [18]. The interaction of thigh and lower leg muscle activation likely
317	
318	
319	
320	2023 Schick et al. Cureus 15(1): e34291. DOI 10.7759/cureus.34291                                                                                                      5 of 8
321	                                                   also plays a role in ACL injuries, especially in non-contact mechanisms [19]. Further research is necessary to
322	                                                  illuminate the interplay of biomechanical forces generated during deceleration on the ACL.
323	
324	
325	                                                  Another factor we correlated with ACL injury, consistent with previous literature, was decreased knee
326	                                                  flexion [8,13]. Biomechanical studies have demonstrated that the greatest degree of strain is placed on the
327	                                                  ACL, relative to other knee ligaments, at low angles of knee flexion (~15°) [20]. When the degree of flexion
328	                                                  increases, the ACL is off-loaded and greater stress is placed on other knee ligaments [21]. A similar study to
329	                                                  that herein found mild knee flexion, defined as 0°-45°, in 82% of ACL injuries in NFL athletes [12]. The high
330	                                                  rate of ACL injury at knee flexion between 0° and 30° (62.3%) observed in our study further supports the
331	                                                  previous video analysis and biomechanical studies [7-9,12,13].
332	
333	
334	                                                  This is the first study to associate foot positioning preceding ACL injury in NFL athletes, as most studies on
335	                                                  sports-related ACL injuries do not assess or highlight initial foot-to-ground contact as a risk factor for injury
336	                                                  [7-9,11-13]. However, a study of rugby players did reveal similar findings with an increased risk of ACL
337	                                                  injuries in players that contact the ground with their heels [10]. Kinematic and biomechanical studies
338	                                                  supported these results, indicating that initial heel strike decreases the dampening forces of the ankle,
339	                                                  thereby transmitting greater forces to the knee [22,23]. Additionally, vibratory forces transmitted to soft
340	                                                  tissue compartments around the knee continue to increase with heel strike, as opposed to plateau with toe
341	                                                  striking [24]. The compounded forces of heel striking may transmit to the ACL preferentially and increase
342	                                                  injury susceptibility.
343	
344	
345	                                                  In contrast to a recent video analysis study of ACL tears in NFL players, our study found that the majority of
346	                                                  ACL injuries occurred via a contact mechanism (58%), including both direct and indirect contact. Johnston et
347	                                                  al. recorded contact mechanisms in only 27.5% of cases; however, 68% of injuries in their study that were
348	                                                  classified as non-contact involved indirect contact [12]. The group considered a contact mechanism only for
349	                                                  those injuries in which there was direct contact with the injured extremity, although they did discuss
350	                                                  indirect “perturbations” as contributing to injuries [12]. We find this noteworthy due to the fact that
351	                                                  distractions, such as blind-sided contact, can alter body motion by impacting muscle activation timing and
352	                                                  thereby influence ACL injury risk [23]. Upper limb motion, such as catching a ball, stiff-arming a defender, or
353	                                                  throwing a pass, has been demonstrated to increase the potential for ACL injury [25]. Indirect contacts
354	                                                  during these actions frequently promote unanticipated reactionary movements by the athlete, such as lateral
355	                                                  trunk abduction, which are highly associated with ACL injury [26].
356	
357	
358	                                                  The high injury rates among receivers and defensive backs in our study are likely multifactorial. These
359	                                                  positions are engaged in the most running, especially at high speeds, with sharp directional and velocity
360	                                                  changes. Such activities have been shown to place increased strain on the ACL and thereby elevate injury
361	                                                  risk [5,6,15]. These positions also frequently collide with other athletes during critical plays. As we and
362	                                                  other studies have noted, more than 50% of ACL injuries in physical sports, such as rugby and American
363	                                                  football, have a contact component [10]. This rate is considerably greater than what is documented in sports
364	                                                  such as basketball (28%) and soccer (36%) [7-9]. Additionally, sport-specific movements can influence ACL
365	                                                  injury frequency. For example, Krosshaug et al. found that 59% of professional basketball players who
366	                                                  suffered an ACL tear did so after landing on their feet from a vertical leap [7]. The same injury pattern was
367	                                                  only observed in 21% of our cases. However, NFL athletes do not jump as frequently as they accelerate and
368	                                                  change direction, although receivers and defensive backs do often leap for catches and pass deflections.
369	                                                  Thus, differences in activity-associated mechanisms between sports make generalizing ACL injury risk
370	                                                  associations very difficult. Lastly, from a non-biomechanical perspective, injuries may be seen at a higher
371	                                                  frequency in the aforementioned positions because they are most likely to be captured on camera, as
372	                                                  technicians focus on ball movement during games. As a result, injuries from linemen or other defensive
373	                                                  players after a pass has been made may go undetected on video and therefore be underrepresented in
374	                                                  studies.
375	
376	
377	                                                  Given the high prevalence of ACL and other ligamentous injuries, prevention strategies should be a major
378	                                                  focus of research. However, there is an absence of literature on the subject in regard to American football
379	                                                  athletes. Most ACL injury prevention training studies have been conducted with soccer athletes. One such
380	                                                  landmark study, Prevent Knee Injury and Enhance Performance (PEP Program), investigated neuromuscular
381	                                                  approaches centered on proprioception exercises and stretching techniques that focus on proper landing
382	                                                  technique, engaging knee and hip flexion on landing and lateral maneuvers, avoiding excessive genu valgum
383	                                                  on landing and squatting, increasing core, hamstring, gluteus medius, and hip abductor strength, and
384	                                                  addressing proper deceleration techniques. Over the two-year trial period, the group of 1,041 high school
385	                                                  female soccer players receiving this training revealed an 88% decrease in anterior cruciate ligament injury
386	                                                  when compared to age- and skill-matched controls in the first year and a 74% reduction during the second
387	                                                  year [27]. Although this study population is not representative of NFL athletes, the principles utilized could
388	                                                  be redirected toward American football-specific drills to serve as a powerful tool in reducing ACL injuries. As
389	                                                  such, there is a definite gap in the literature that needs to be addressed; the results from injury prevention
390	                                                  training programs on American football, along with other contact sports, may not only reduce short-term
391	                                                  ligamentous injury risk but also pay dividends by reducing long-term joint damage from post-traumatic
392	                                                  osteoarthritis [28].
393	
394	
395	
396	
397	2023 Schick et al. Cureus 15(1): e34291. DOI 10.7759/cureus.34291                                                                                                     6 of 8
398	                                                   Limitations
399	                                                  This study is not without limitations. Only a small percentage of ACL injuries that occurred among NFL
400	                                                  players (12%) had associated videos available for analysis. Injury rates among the various positions may be
401	                                                  influenced by which positions are in the camera’s spotlight, as videographers focus on ball movement during
402	                                                  plays. Since we only used publicly available videos and did not use any paid subscription service or obtain
403	                                                  videos from individual NFL teams, the percentage of athletes studied was lower than the study conducted by
404	                                                  Johnston et al. Further access to such videos would likely alter our results. Also, these videos were produced
405	                                                  for fan viewership and not for kinematic analysis. Despite this, there was high agreement between the video
406	                                                  data collectors. Given that we performed a descriptive study, a detailed causation analysis could not be
407	                                                  performed. This is due to the fact that video analysis alone cannot be used to assess ACL forces generated by
408	                                                  various movements.
409	
410	
411	                                                  Conclusions
412	                                                  Most ACL injuries in NFL athletes are associated with contact, brisk deceleration, and shallow knee and hip
413	                                                  flexion angles. Additionally, heel strike is a major kinematic risk factor for injury in this player population.
414	                                                  Given the heterogeneity of movements between sports, these conclusions cannot be applied broadly across
415	                                                  sports, but an awareness of such associated activities should guide preventative training methods and
416	                                                  research to lower ligamentous injuries in athletes.

                                                Abstract
                                                Introduction
                                                Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are common among American football athletes, although few
                                                studies have performed video analyses of ACL injuries to better understand the injury mechanism. This work
                                                aims to characterize the mechanism of ACL injury during professional football competitions using video
                                                analysis. We hypothesize that football-specific injury trends will emerge, including high rates of contact
                                                injuries and associations with shallow knee and hip flexion angles (0°-30°).


                                                Methods
                                                Videos of professional football players suffering ACL injuries from 2007 to 2016 were analyzed. Injured
                                                players were identified using the injured reserve (IR) lists of the National Football League (NFL), and videos
                                                were discovered via a systematic Google search. Descriptive statistics and frequency analyses were
                                                performed on all variables using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) version 23.0 (IBM SPSS
                                                Statistics, Armonk, NY, USA).


                                                Results
                                                Of the 429 ACL injuries identified, 53 (12%) videos were available. Deceleration was the most common injury
                                                maneuver, present in 32 (60%) athletes. Thirty-one (58%) players suffered contact injuries. Twenty-eight
                                                (53%) injuries demonstrated valgus collapse of the knee, and 26 (49%) had neutral knee rotation. Defensive
                                                backs (26%) and wide receivers (23%) were the most frequently injured positions.


                                                Conclusion
                                                Overall, we found that most ACL injuries had preceding contact, deceleration, shallow hip and knee flexion,
                                                and heel strike, and subsequent valgus collapse and neutral knee rotation. This understanding of American
                                                football-specific ACL tear mechanisms could help direct the focus of future injury prevention training
                                                modalities.



                                                Categories: Orthopedics
                                                Keywords: risk factor, american football, nfl, video analysis, acl injury



                                                Introduction
                                                Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears are devastating injuries in professional athletes, affecting
                                                approximately 4% of players each year. ACL injuries are particularly impactful on the careers of athletes in
                                                the National Football League (NFL), with studies demonstrating a return to play rate of 63%-82% and a
                                                salary decrease of $2 million over the following four seasons when compared to their uninjured counterparts
                                                [1-3]. It has been shown that these injuries are associated with many different movements, such as pivoting,
                                                cutting, jumping, accelerating, and decelerating [4,5]. Understanding the risk factors and mechanisms
                                                correlated with ACL injuries is important in injury prevention [6].


                                                Recent studies have performed video analyses of basketball, European football (soccer), netball, alpine
                                                skiing, Australian football, rugby, and American football players suffering ACL injuries with the goal of
                                                highlighting trends in injury mechanism and knee biomechanics before and after injury [7-11]. These studies
                                                found that in non-contact sports, the three predominant forms of injury mechanism were landing from
                                                jumping, decelerating, and cutting maneuvers. Valgus collapse was also frequently found following injury


                               How to cite this article
                               Schick S, Cantrell C K, Young B, et al. (January 27, 2023) The Mechanism of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries in the National Football League: A
                               Systematic Video Review. Cureus 15(1): e34291. DOI 10.7759/cureus.34291
                                                   [11]. Johnston et al. performed a similar study investigating ACL injuries in professional football players.
                                                  However, despite football being a contact sport, the authors noted that most ACL injuries were non-contact
                                                  and associated with lateral movement and knee flexion of 0°-45° [12].


                                                  In this study, we sought to perform a similar video analysis of ACL injuries in NFL players, with the aim of
                                                  determining the predominant ACL injury mechanisms in American football. Additionally, we aimed to
                                                  describe the kinematics immediately before and after ACL injury to better understand the forces directed
                                                  upon the knee causing injury. We hypothesized that most injuries would be contact-related and occur during
                                                  abrupt changes in stride and that athletes would be positioned in shallow knee and hip flexion (0°-30°).


                                                  Materials And Methods
                                                  NFL injured reserve (IR) lists from 2007 to 2016 were reviewed (https://www.foxsports.com/nfl/transactions)
                                                  (access date: September 25, 2017). Any player whose injury description included the words “leg,” “knee,” or
                                                  “ACL” was further investigated to determine whether an ACL injury occurred. Once ACL injury was confirmed
                                                  via injury reports, player profiles/biographies, or press releases, videos of the injuries were accessed via a
                                                  systematic Google search using the keywords “Player Name” and “ACL Injury Video.” The first five pages of
                                                  results were viewed. There was no minimum number of video angles required; however, most videos
                                                  provided more than one for injury analysis. Videos were qualified for review if all data points were
                                                  visualized. Player demographics such as height, weight, position, age, and race were obtained from NFL.com
                                                  player rosters.


                                                  Three authors independently reviewed and analyzed the videos. The collected data points included the
                                                  following: horizontal running speed, vertical running speed, acceleration/deceleration/constant speed,
                                                  player maneuver, player contact (direct/indirect), foot-to-ground contact, knee flexion angle, hip flexion
                                                  angle, ankle dorsiflexion/plantar flexion, direction of knee collapse, and direction of rotation upon collapse.
                                                  Joint flexion angles were stratified into 30° intervals to accurately categorize flexion angles for analysis.
                                                  Additional definitions of injury-associated characteristics can be found in Table 1.

                                                    Acceleration, deceleration, or constant speed was determined in the time immediately preceding injury.
                                                    Player contact was determined if there was any contact from another player at the time of injury. Direct
                                                    contact was defined as contact directly to the injured knee. Indirect contact was defined as any contact to
                                                    the body other than the injured knee. Foot-to-ground contact (toe versus heel strike) was determined by
                                                    which portion of the foot struck the ground first at or immediately prior to injury. Data were combined, and
                                                    all discrepancies were settled via a collective agreement between the reviewers. The authors’ agreement
                                                    equaled 96% for collected data points before reconciliation.


                                                    Descriptive statistics were performed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) version 23.0
                                                    (IBM SPSS Statistics, Armonk, NY, USA). Frequencies of all categorical variables were gathered. Additionally,
                                                    descriptive statistics were performed for all continuous variables.


                                                    Results
                                                    Over the year period, 429 ACL injuries were identified via the NFL’s IR lists. Of these injuries, publicly
                                                    accessible videos were available for 53 (12%). The average age for injured players was 27±3 years. Defensive
                                                    backs and wide receivers sustained the most injuries, with 14 (26%) and 12 (23%), respectively. Forty-four
                                                    (83%) were first-time ACL injuries, while nine (17%) had experienced a previous injury. Complete player
                                                    demographics are available in Table 2.

                                                    Shallow flexion was the most common joint positioning observed among injured athletes. Thirty-three (62%)
                                                    injuries occurred at 0°-30° knee flexion, 26 (49%) were at 0°-30° hip flexion, and 28 (53%) were at 0°-30° of
                                                    plantar flexion. The predominant rotation pattern was neutral with 26 (49%) injuries, while valgus
                                                    directional collapse was noted in 28 (53%) injuries. Full results for lower extremity joint flexion angles,
                                                    collapse, and rotation upon collapse can be found in Table 3.


                                                    Out of the nine athletes with a prior knee injury, six (66%) experienced an ACL injury on the previously
                                                    repaired knee, four of which were associated with contact (two direct and two indirect). Five (83%) players
                                                    were decelerating during injury, and four (67%) were landing when injured. Initial heel and toe strikes were
                                                    even at three (50%) each, and five injuries (83%) occurred with plantar flexion of the ankle and half (3) with
                                                    mild knee and hip flexion.


                                                    Discussion
                                                    This study aimed to use video analysis to assess trends in the ACL injury mechanisms of American football
                                                    players. The kinematics most commonly encountered with ACL injuries were deceleration, mild knee flexion
                                                    (0°-30°), and initial foot-to-ground contact through heel strike. Additionally, most injuries were associated
                                                    with contact from another athlete, either directly to the knee or indirectly to other parts of the body.


                                                    Similar to previous soccer literature, most players we analyzed were decelerating at the time of injury [13].
                                                    However, this is discordant with Johnston et al., who previously noted that only 10% of ACL injuries in
                                                    professional American football players were associated with deceleration [12]. Unfortunately, the majority of
                                                    video analyses of sports-related injuries do not assess this crucial injury characteristic. Numerous studies
                                                    have examined the forces placed on the ACL during a single-leg landing during various actions and
                                                    confirmed that increased tension is placed on the ACL during deceleration [14-16]. Several hypotheses have
                                                    been proposed to explain this biomechanical correlation. One theory purports that deceleration places
                                                    substantial stress on the ACL in an effort to prevent anterior tibial translation [17]. Another asserts that
                                                    eccentric quadriceps contraction, as with deceleration, increases the compressive vector within the knee,
                                                    effectively lowering the injury threshold [18]. The interaction of thigh and lower leg muscle activation likely



2023 Schick et al. Cureus 15(1): e34291. DOI 10.7759/cureus.34291                                                                                                      5 of 8
                                                   also plays a role in ACL injuries, especially in non-contact mechanisms [19]. Further research is necessary to
                                                  illuminate the interplay of biomechanical forces generated during deceleration on the ACL.


                                                  Another factor we correlated with ACL injury, consistent with previous literature, was decreased knee
                                                  flexion [8,13]. Biomechanical studies have demonstrated that the greatest degree of strain is placed on the
                                                  ACL, relative to other knee ligaments, at low angles of knee flexion (~15°) [20]. When the degree of flexion
                                                  increases, the ACL is off-loaded and greater stress is placed on other knee ligaments [21]. A similar study to
                                                  that herein found mild knee flexion, defined as 0°-45°, in 82% of ACL injuries in NFL athletes [12]. The high
                                                  rate of ACL injury at knee flexion between 0° and 30° (62.3%) observed in our study further supports the
                                                  previous video analysis and biomechanical studies [7-9,12,13].


                                                  This is the first study to associate foot positioning preceding ACL injury in NFL athletes, as most studies on
                                                  sports-related ACL injuries do not assess or highlight initial foot-to-ground contact as a risk factor for injury
                                                  [7-9,11-13]. However, a study of rugby players did reveal similar findings with an increased risk of ACL
                                                  injuries in players that contact the ground with their heels [10]. Kinematic and biomechanical studies
                                                  supported these results, indicating that initial heel strike decreases the dampening forces of the ankle,
                                                  thereby transmitting greater forces to the knee [22,23]. Additionally, vibratory forces transmitted to soft
                                                  tissue compartments around the knee continue to increase with heel strike, as opposed to plateau with toe
                                                  striking [24]. The compounded forces of heel striking may transmit to the ACL preferentially and increase
                                                  injury susceptibility.


                                                  In contrast to a recent video analysis study of ACL tears in NFL players, our study found that the majority of
                                                  ACL injuries occurred via a contact mechanism (58%), including both direct and indirect contact. Johnston et
                                                  al. recorded contact mechanisms in only 27.5% of cases; however, 68% of injuries in their study that were
                                                  classified as non-contact involved indirect contact [12]. The group considered a contact mechanism only for
                                                  those injuries in which there was direct contact with the injured extremity, although they did discuss
                                                  indirect “perturbations” as contributing to injuries [12]. We find this noteworthy due to the fact that
                                                  distractions, such as blind-sided contact, can alter body motion by impacting muscle activation timing and
                                                  thereby influence ACL injury risk [23]. Upper limb motion, such as catching a ball, stiff-arming a defender, or
                                                  throwing a pass, has been demonstrated to increase the potential for ACL injury [25]. Indirect contacts
                                                  during these actions frequently promote unanticipated reactionary movements by the athlete, such as lateral
                                                  trunk abduction, which are highly associated with ACL injury [26].


                                                  The high injury rates among receivers and defensive backs in our study are likely multifactorial. These
                                                  positions are engaged in the most running, especially at high speeds, with sharp directional and velocity
                                                  changes. Such activities have been shown to place increased strain on the ACL and thereby elevate injury
                                                  risk [5,6,15]. These positions also frequently collide with other athletes during critical plays. As we and
                                                  other studies have noted, more than 50% of ACL injuries in physical sports, such as rugby and American
                                                  football, have a contact component [10]. This rate is considerably greater than what is documented in sports
                                                  such as basketball (28%) and soccer (36%) [7-9]. Additionally, sport-specific movements can influence ACL
                                                  injury frequency. For example, Krosshaug et al. found that 59% of professional basketball players who
                                                  suffered an ACL tear did so after landing on their feet from a vertical leap [7]. The same injury pattern was
                                                  only observed in 21% of our cases. However, NFL athletes do not jump as frequently as they accelerate and
                                                  change direction, although receivers and defensive backs do often leap for catches and pass deflections.
                                                  Thus, differences in activity-associated mechanisms between sports make generalizing ACL injury risk
                                                  associations very difficult. Lastly, from a non-biomechanical perspective, injuries may be seen at a higher
                                                  frequency in the aforementioned positions because they are most likely to be captured on camera, as
                                                  technicians focus on ball movement during games. As a result, injuries from linemen or other defensive
                                                  players after a pass has been made may go undetected on video and therefore be underrepresented in
                                                  studies.


                                                  Given the high prevalence of ACL and other ligamentous injuries, prevention strategies should be a major
                                                  focus of research. However, there is an absence of literature on the subject in regard to American football
                                                  athletes. Most ACL injury prevention training studies have been conducted with soccer athletes. One such
                                                  landmark study, Prevent Knee Injury and Enhance Performance (PEP Program), investigated neuromuscular
                                                  approaches centered on proprioception exercises and stretching techniques that focus on proper landing
                                                  technique, engaging knee and hip flexion on landing and lateral maneuvers, avoiding excessive genu valgum
                                                  on landing and squatting, increasing core, hamstring, gluteus medius, and hip abductor strength, and
                                                  addressing proper deceleration techniques. Over the two-year trial period, the group of 1,041 high school
                                                  female soccer players receiving this training revealed an 88% decrease in anterior cruciate ligament injury
                                                  when compared to age- and skill-matched controls in the first year and a 74% reduction during the second
                                                  year [27]. Although this study population is not representative of NFL athletes, the principles utilized could
                                                  be redirected toward American football-specific drills to serve as a powerful tool in reducing ACL injuries. As
                                                  such, there is a definite gap in the literature that needs to be addressed; the results from injury prevention
                                                  training programs on American football, along with other contact sports, may not only reduce short-term
                                                  ligamentous injury risk but also pay dividends by reducing long-term joint damage from post-traumatic
                                                  osteoarthritis [28].

                                                   Limitations
                                                  This study is not without limitations. Only a small percentage of ACL injuries that occurred among NFL
                                                  players (12%) had associated videos available for analysis. Injury rates among the various positions may be
                                                  influenced by which positions are in the camera’s spotlight, as videographers focus on ball movement during
                                                  plays. Since we only used publicly available videos and did not use any paid subscription service or obtain
                                                  videos from individual NFL teams, the percentage of athletes studied was lower than the study conducted by
                                                  Johnston et al. Further access to such videos would likely alter our results. Also, these videos were produced
                                                  for fan viewership and not for kinematic analysis. Despite this, there was high agreement between the video
                                                  data collectors. Given that we performed a descriptive study, a detailed causation analysis could not be
                                                  performed. This is due to the fact that video analysis alone cannot be used to assess ACL forces generated by
                                                  various movements.


                                                  Conclusions
                                                  Most ACL injuries in NFL athletes are associated with contact, brisk deceleration, and shallow knee and hip
                                                  flexion angles. Additionally, heel strike is a major kinematic risk factor for injury in this player population.
                                                  Given the heterogeneity of movements between sports, these conclusions cannot be applied broadly across
                                                  sports, but an awareness of such associated activities should guide preventative training methods and
                                                  research to lower ligamentous injuries in athletes.

11	Adam Danielsson1,2, Alexandra Horvath3, Carl Senorski1, Eduard Alentorn-Geli4,5,6, William E. Garrett7,

15	  Abstract
16	  Background: Injuries to the hamstring muscles are among the most common in sports and account for significant
17	  time loss. Despite being so common, the injury mechanism of hamstring injuries remains to be determined.
18	  Purpose: To investigate the hamstring injury mechanism by conducting a systematic review.
19	  Study design: A systematic review following the PRISMA statement.
20	  Methods: A systematic search was conducted using PubMed, EMBASE and the Cochrane Library. Studies 1) written
21	  in English and 2) deciding on the mechanism of hamstring injury were eligible for inclusion. Literature reviews,
22	  systematic reviews, meta-analyses, conference abstracts, book chapters and editorials were excluded, as well as
23	  studies where the full text could not be obtained.
24	  Results: Twenty-six of 2372 screened original studies were included and stratified to the mechanism or
25	  methods used to determine hamstring injury: stretch-related injuries, kinematic analysis, electromyography-based
26	  kinematic analysis and strength-related injuries. All studies that reported the stretch-type injury mechanism
27	  concluded that injury occurs due to extensive hip flexion with a hyperextended knee. The vast majority of
28	  studies on injuries during running proposed that these injuries occur during the late swing phase of the
29	  running gait cycle.
30	  Conclusion: A stretch-type injury to the hamstrings is caused by extensive hip flexion with an extended
31	  knee. Hamstring injuries during sprinting are most likely to occur due to excessive muscle strain caused by
32	  eccentric contraction during the late swing phase of the running gait cycle.
33	  Level of evidence: Level IV
34	  Keywords: Running, Sprinting, Biomechanics, Strength, Muscle injury

The mechanism of hamstring injuries – a
systematic review
Adam Danielsson1,2, Alexandra Horvath3, Carl Senorski1, Eduard Alentorn-Geli4,5,6, William E. Garrett7,
Ramón Cugat4,5,6, Kristian Samuelsson1,2 and Eric Hamrin Senorski2,8*


  Abstract
  Background: Injuries to the hamstring muscles are among the most common in sports and account for significant
  time loss. Despite being so common, the injury mechanism of hamstring injuries remains to be determined.
  Purpose: To investigate the hamstring injury mechanism by conducting a systematic review.
  Study design: A systematic review following the PRISMA statement.
  Methods: A systematic search was conducted using PubMed, EMBASE and the Cochrane Library. Studies 1) written
  in English and 2) deciding on the mechanism of hamstring injury were eligible for inclusion. Literature reviews,
  systematic reviews, meta-analyses, conference abstracts, book chapters and editorials were excluded, as well as
  studies where the full text could not be obtained.
  Results: Twenty-six of 2372 screened original studies were included and stratified to the mechanism or
  methods used to determine hamstring injury: stretch-related injuries, kinematic analysis, electromyography-based
  kinematic analysis and strength-related injuries. All studies that reported the stretch-type injury mechanism
  concluded that injury occurs due to extensive hip flexion with a hyperextended knee. The vast majority of
  studies on injuries during running proposed that these injuries occur during the late swing phase of the
  running gait cycle.
  Conclusion: A stretch-type injury to the hamstrings is caused by extensive hip flexion with an extended
  knee. Hamstring injuries during sprinting are most likely to occur due to excessive muscle strain caused by
  eccentric contraction during the late swing phase of the running gait cycle.
  Level of evidence: Level IV
  Keywords: Running, Sprinting, Biomechanics, Strength, Muscle injury

 "evidenceSummary":"This PRISMA systematic review searched PubMed, EMBASE and the Cochrane Library and included 26 original studies on hamstring injury mechanisms, covering stretch-type injuries (3 studies), kinematic analysis (10), kinematic plus EMG analysis (10) and strength-related injuries (3). Stretch-type injuries were attributed to extensive hip flexion with knee extension, and most running-related studies placed injury in the late swing phase. Most included studies had small samples and estimated mechanisms in uninjured people, and the reported quality was low (median Downs and Black score 8 of 20).",

   "doi":"10.1186/s12891-020-03658-8",
   "abstract":"Hamstring injuries are common in sport, but their mechanism is not agreed. This PRISMA systematic review of 26 original studies classified the evidence by method: stretch-related injuries, kinematic analysis, electromyography-based kinematic analysis and strength-related injuries. Studies of stretch-type injury concluded that injury occurs with extensive hip flexion and an extended knee. Most studies of running injury proposed the late swing phase of the gait cycle, where eccentric muscle strain is greatest.",
   "tldr":"Stretch-type hamstring injuries seem to happen with the hip strongly flexed and the knee straight, and running injuries are most often linked to the late swing phase. The evidence is mostly small, low-quality studies, so treat these mechanisms as working hypotheses.",
   "methods":"Systematic review following PRISMA. PubMed, EMBASE and Cochrane Library were searched (2017 to 2019) for English-language original studies on hamstring injury mechanisms or hamstring biomechanics. Two authors screened and extracted data independently, and study quality was rated with a modified Downs and Black checklist. Results were synthesised qualitatively by method group.",
   "findings":"Of 26 included studies, three (dancers and water skiers, 12 to 30 people) reported stretch-type injuries from extensive hip flexion with knee extension. Among running studies, seven kinematic studies placed injury in the swing phase and two in the early stance phase, and most EMG-kinematic studies also placed it in swing. Strength studies in football players found fatigue-related lower eccentric endurance in previously injured players. Median study quality was 8 of 20. Only six studies analysed actual injuries, and in several of those the injury was recalled by the patient.",
   "limitations":"The authors note that the included studies are small, often with one or two runners, and that most estimate the mechanism in uninjured people. Quality scores were low (median 8 of 20). Two of the real-time injury studies used the same participant. The abstract reports 2372 screened studies, while the results section reports 2841 screened after duplicates were removed, a discrepancy in the reported numbers.",
   "practicalImplications":"The review supports including hip and core control and eccentric hamstring loading in prevention work, and the late swing phase is the most consistent running mechanism reported. Because most evidence is estimated rather than observed, programme choices should be checked against athlete monitoring and clinical findings rather than treated as proven.",
   "athleteDev":"For sprinting and running athletes, the review supports eccentric hamstring strength and hip and core control as areas to address in training. It does not show which specific exercise reduces hamstring injury rates.",
   "rtp":"The review addresses injury mechanism, not return to sport. It cannot be used to set return-to-running or sprint clearance criteria, although its findings on stretch injuries and late swing may inform rehabilitation exercise choice."
 }
}

 "evidenceSummary":"This narrative review discusses the types of recovery after exercise and summarises the reported effects of common methods (cold water immersion, cryotherapy, massage, foam rolling, compression, stretching, and nutrition such as protein, creatine and BCAAs) on soreness, creatine kinase, strength and performance. No systematic search method is described.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The review does not describe how sources were chosen, and the effect sizes in its table come from meta-analyses of mixed sports and populations. The worked example is a small illustrative study whose individual data are shown but not analysed statistically in the text.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the summarised effects of cold water immersion or creatine as reliable for their own athletes, when the table reflects mixed populations and the individual-response argument is a conceptual proposal.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2023,
   "citation":"Rappelt L, Javanmardi S, Heinke L, Baumgart C, Freiwald J, et al. The multifaceted nature of recovery after exercise: A need for individualization. Sports Orthop. Traumatol. 2023.",
   "doi":"10.1016/j.orthtr.2023.10.006",
   "abstract":"Balancing training load and recovery is important for adaptation and for avoiding overuse injury. Recovery has physical and psychological aspects, and different measures recover over different time spans. The authors argue that group-based evidence from randomised trials needs to be combined with repeated individual measurements to choose recovery methods for an athlete. The review summarises the reported effects of common recovery methods and discusses how to test them at the individual level, for example with Bayesian approaches and repeated testing.",
   "tldr":"Recovery is not one measure and does not follow one time course, and group averages from trials may not fit an individual athlete. Combine group evidence with an athlete's own repeated measures before choosing a recovery method.",
   "methods":"Narrative review and special-issue article. The authors describe the physiological and psychological factors of recovery, summarise effect sizes from published meta-analyses of recovery methods in a table, and illustrate individual variation with data from a recent group study (cold water immersion, percussive massage and passive rest groups, 10 to 11 participants each). No systematic search method is described.",
   "findings":"Table 1 reports that cold water immersion and cryotherapy reduce soreness and creatine kinase in several studies, with effects varying by time frame. Foam rolling, stick massage and pressotherapy showed no significant effect on range of motion, swelling, strength or jump performance in the reviewed studies, although foam rolling showed a non-significant trend toward better strength recovery. Compression garments improved strength in the first 24 hours, and protein and creatine reduced creatine kinase in several meta-analyses. The illustrative group study showed large method-by-time interaction effects, especially immediately after the recovery protocol, with large individual differences in time course.",
   "limitations":"The review does not state a search strategy or inclusion criteria, and the table draws on studies with different populations, durations and outcomes. Small elite samples limit power, and group-mean findings may not apply to individuals. The authors note that inflammation and damage markers do not follow the same time course as performance recovery.",
   "practicalImplications":"Choose recovery methods by the goal and time available, such as soreness relief after a match or strength recovery within 24 hours. Use repeated measures on each athlete, such as creatine kinase, jump height or perceived muscle stiffness, to see whether a method works for that person, rather than relying on group averages alone.",
   "athleteDev":"Recovery choice should follow the training phase and the next session or competition. Individual monitoring is needed to show whether an intervention helps a given athlete.",
   "rtp":"The review addresses recovery after training and competition, not injury rehabilitation or return to sport. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria."
 }
}

comparable to previously published investigations utilising similar measurements in analogous

populations (21-23). Both sprint groups demonstrated relatively large muscle volumes when



A
compared with previous studies, however comparison to previous literature is confounded by

differences in performance standard, the inclusion of both male and female sprinters in some

studies (5) and potential ethnic differences (7). The performance standard of the elite sprinters in

this study (n=5; SBE100 10.03 – 10.21 s; PBE100 9.91 – 10.08 s) were all faster than any

mechanistic reason for the greater muscularity of elite > sub-elite > controls in the current study,

are not possible to discern from this investigation, although it seems likely that the sprint and

               C
resistance training history of the groups, which shows a similar pattern, would contribute to these



  C
differences in muscularity.

                            EP

                              TE
flexors facilitate the application of horizontal forces to the ground (26), and thus these muscle

groups are considered critical for propulsion (27). Whereas, the hip flexors are thought crucial to

the rapid acceleration of the legs during swing phase in order to achieve high stride frequencies

groups.

  C

A

0.639). The largest previous study of muscle morphology in sub-elite sprinters also reported the

                              TE

                              TE

{
 "id":"Q22",
 "sourceFile":"The muscle morphology of elite sprint running.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Text title 'The Muscle Morphology of Elite Sprint Running' matches the filename; the article's own DOI 10.1249/MSS.0000000000002522 is printed in the header (accepted manuscript, published ahead of print).",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Training & Performance",
 "domains":["Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Research & Analytics","Coaching"],
 "sports":["Track & Field"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Professional / Elite","Healthy Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"This cross-sectional study used 3T MRI to measure lower-limb muscle volumes and isometric strength in 5 elite male sprinters, 26 sub-elite male sprinters and 11 untrained male controls. Elite sprinters had 48% more total muscle volume than controls and 24% more than sub-elite sprinters, with the hip extensors (+32% absolute, +15% relative to body mass vs sub-elite) and gluteus maximus the clearest differences. Gluteus maximus volume was the strongest single correlate of 100 m season's-best time (r = -0.639) and isometric strength did not separate the two sprint groups.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The elite group is only five athletes, so the group differences and correlations rest on a very small sample. The design is cross-sectional with no cause-and-effect evidence, and the sub-elite 100 m times were estimated from 60 or 200 m results for 7 of 26 athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read gluteus maximus and hip extensor size as a target that makes sprinters faster, when the study shows association in a five-athlete elite group and cannot show that building these muscles improves sprint times.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020,
   "citation":"Miller R, Balshaw TG, Massey GJ, Maeo S, Lanza MB, Johnston M, et al. The Muscle Morphology of Elite Sprint Running. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2020. Published ahead of print.",
   "doi":"10.1249/MSS.0000000000002522",
   "abstract":"This cross-sectional study compared lower-limb muscle volumes (3T MRI) and isometric strength between 5 elite sprinters (100 m season's best 10.10 ± 0.07 s), 26 sub-elite sprinters and 11 untrained controls, and related these to sprint performance. Total lower-body muscularity was greater in elite than sub-elite sprinters and controls. Hip extensor and gluteus maximus volumes differentiated elite from sub-elite sprinters and correlated with sprint times. Isometric strength was greater in both sprint groups than controls but did not differ between sprint groups or relate to performance.",
   "tldr":"Elite sprinters carried more muscle than sub-elite sprinters, especially in the hip extensors and gluteus maximus, and those muscles tracked sprint time. Strength tests did not separate the groups, and the elite group was only five athletes.",
   "methods":"Cross-sectional study with two sessions per participant: isometric strength of five functional muscle groups on custom dynamometers, and 3T MRI for volumes of 23 lower-limb muscles or compartments (manual segmentation, 6 blinded analysts). Performance was 100 m season's-best equivalent (SBE100) from IAAF points. Groups were compared with one-way ANOVA and Bonferroni post-hoc tests; SBE100 was correlated with volumes and strength (Pearson, Benjamini-Hochberg correction), and stepwise regression estimated variance explained.",
   "findings":"Total unilateral muscle volume was 48% greater in elite than controls and 20% greater in sub-elite than controls, and 24% greater in elite than sub-elite sprinters. Elite sprinters had greater absolute hip extensor volume (+32%) than sub-elite sprinters, and relative hip extensor volume was +15%. Gluteus maximus (+45% absolute), TFL and sartorius were larger in elite than sub-elite sprinters. Gluteus maximus volume explained 43.8% of the variance in SBE100 (absolute volume), and hip extensor volume explained 47.5%. Isometric strength was greater in sprinters than controls in several groups but did not differ between sprint groups, and only relative knee extensor strength correlated with SBE100, in the unexpected direction (r = 0.485).",
   "limitations":"The authors note that the elite group had only five athletes, that isometric strength was measured once without familiarisation, and that strength tests may lack specificity to fast sprinting. Strength and performance were measured at different times, and some sub-elite 100 m times were estimated from 60 or 200 m results. The cross-sectional design cannot establish cause and effect, although the authors argue a causal component is likely.",
   "practicalImplications":"Coaches could consider hip extensor and gluteus maximus development as a target for sprint athletes, since these were the largest group and individual muscle differences in this sample. The authors note that the exercises needed to develop the TFL, sartorius and gluteus maximus specifically are not well established. Athletes with large gluteus maximus volume may not be faster, so these findings should inform training choices rather than set individual targets.",
   "athleteDev":"For sprinters, the study supports including exercises that build hip extensor and knee flexor size, such as heavy resistance training, as part of performance development. It does not show which exercises produce the largest gains in those muscles or in sprint speed.",
   "rtp":"The study is in healthy, uninjured athletes and does not address return to sport. It cannot be used to set return-to-sprint criteria after injury."
 }
}
